953.title: The Pali Text Society
953.hook: founded 1881 to publish the texts; the translations we read here began there
953.howItsDone: Students and scholars of the Pali tradition read and cite the texts in the editions and translations of the Pali Text Society, alongside newer translations, and monasteries keep chanting the texts in Pali.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a week of crossings ended with temples on far continents. Your line: a good man pervades every place.

Look under the quotations on this path and two names keep turning up. Max Müller, for the Dhammapada. And Rhys Davids, for the suttas. "Thus have I heard." The Buddha's last words. The advice to be a lamp to yourself. Those English sentences came to us through Rhys Davids' hands and the hands of the people he worked with. Behind them stands an unlikely thing: a society, set up in London by scholars, with a plain goal. Print the Pali texts so anyone could read them, and put them into English.
screen: `ONE NAME UNDER THE QUOTES.` → `A SOCIETY IN LONDON.` → `PRINT THE TEXTS.`

segments.voice: We met T. W. Rhys Davids a few days back, among the first translators. He had worked in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, as a British official. Accounts say he first learned Pali there, from a Sri Lankan monk, so he could read old documents in court. He came home wanting the texts he had met to be open to everyone. So he founded the Pali Text Society, to edit the Pali texts and print them in roman letters. Before that, they lived mainly in palm-leaf manuscripts in monasteries in Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand, in local scripts. The work was never one person's. Scholars in Europe and Asia edited texts side by side, comparing manuscripts. Monks in Asia lent manuscripts and answered questions. Caroline Rhys Davids, his wife, translated and edited, and later led the society herself. Then came translations. Rhys Davids' Dialogues of the Buddha opens its first sutta with: "Thus have I heard." Every translation is a set of choices, and later translators have made different ones. The society still publishes, and scholars still find their way around the Pali texts by the volume and page numbers of its editions. Here, we read what the translators handed us.
screen: `RHYS DAVIDS LEARNS PALI.` · `A SOCIETY TO PRINT THE TEXTS.` · `MANY HANDS, MANY MANUSCRIPTS.` · `INTO ENGLISH.` · then, large: `THE TRANSLATORS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one line from this path that stayed with you, thus have I heard, maybe, or a verse of the Dhammapada, and think back along the chain it traveled: the monks who memorized it, the scribes who wrote it on palm leaves, the editors who compared copies, the translators who chose each English word. You don't know most of their names; silently, thank them anyway. Then rest with the line itself.
Rhys Davids. The British official who learned Pali in Ceylon and founded the society that printed the Pali texts and put them into English.
Your line: the translators. Behind every line here, many hands. Day nine hundred fifty-three, done.

954.title: Practice online
954.hook: talks, chanting and sittings now travel by screen
954.howItsDone: Buddhist temples and meditation centers stream talks, chanting and group sittings, and practitioners join from home, alongside or instead of sitting in person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rhys Davids, the Pali Text Society, and the people behind the page. Your line: the translators.

A laptop propped on a stack of books. On the screen, a grid of small windows: a woman by a candle, a man in a parked car, an older monk in a robe, someone whose cat keeps walking across the keyboard. A bell rings through tinny speakers, and every face in every window closes its eyes at once, in different rooms, in different time zones. Nobody says a word for a long while. Then the bell again, and a few people wave.
screen: `A GRID OF SMALL WINDOWS.` → `ONE BELL, MANY ROOMS.` → `EYES CLOSE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: A dharma talk used to reach the people in the room. Now teachers record their talks, and students listen on a commute or while washing dishes, sometimes years later and continents away. A hall in Chicago held the speakers we met last week; a phone holds talks from the schools we've met on this road. Temples and monasteries stream their morning chanting and their services, so someone at a kitchen table can chant the refuges in Pali, or the Heart Sutra, along with a monastery they've never visited. Why does company matter? In the Pali texts, the Buddha's attendant Ananda once said that good friendship, good companions, must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrected him. Not half: good friendship is the whole of the holy life. That's the Upaddha Sutta, in the Samyutta Nikaya. Online sitting is one way people try to keep that kind of company when a temple is far away, or when they're sick, caring for someone, or can't leave home. Teachers differ. Some welcome online sittings and teach on screen every week. Others say some things only happen in a shared room: the smell of incense, a teacher noticing your posture, a bow you can actually see. Some communities do both. The texts don't settle that question. What they do say is that company on the path matters.
screen: `TALKS THAT TRAVEL.` · `CHANTING CARRIED HOME.` · `GOOD FRIENDSHIP IS THE WHOLE.` · `TEACHERS DIFFER.` · then, large: `SITTING TOGETHER, APART.`

segments.voice: Practice the part that makes a group sitting work, starting and stopping together: when the bell rings, settle at once, without fidgeting into it, and let your breath go at its own pace. When it rings again, stop where you are, open your eyes, and give a small nod, the way people wave in the grid.
Practice online. Talks, chanting and sittings that travel by screen, so people far apart can keep company on the path.
Your line: sitting together, apart. Not half the path: the whole of it. See you tomorrow.

955.title: The northern roads, closed
955.hook: China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, Mongolia, the West
955.howItsDone: Buddhists in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Tibet, Mongolia and the West each keep the forms the teaching took on its way to them, and pilgrims still travel these roads to the temples and sites along them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: practice online, faces in small windows and one bell. Your line: sitting together, apart.

A tongue that would not burn. Water drunk from a skull in the dark. A bronze Buddha on a ship. Two niches in a cliff, holding nothing. A palace on a hill. A cup of tea running over the rim. A few of the things this path has picked up on one long road: from the tree in northern India north over the mountains, east to the sea, up onto the plateau, out to the grasslands, and across an ocean to Chicago.
screen: `A TONGUE, A SKULL, A SHIP.` → `ONE LONG ROAD.` → `ACROSS AN OCEAN.`

segments.voice: Monks and merchants carried the teaching along the caravan roads of the Silk Road. Kumarajiva translated sutras into Chinese, and the story says his tongue did not burn. Faxian walked to India, and Xuanzang crossed the desert, tradition says against the emperor's ban, and came home with the texts. Bodhidharma, the story goes, told an emperor his temples earned no merit, and a woodcutter named Huineng, who couldn't write, asked someone to put his verse on a wall. Guanyin heard the cries of the world. In Korea, Wonhyo drank water from a skull in the dark and woke up to his own mind. The whole canon was carved into woodblocks, and carved again after a fire. A bronze Buddha crossed the sea from Korea to Japan; the great Buddha rose at Nara; monks climbed Mount Hiei and Koyasan, and new schools grew. In Tibet, a king invited an abbot; Padmasambhava came; Samye was built; a debate was held. After the quiet years, a translator walked to India, Atisha came, and the canons were gathered. A line of Dalai Lamas, a palace on a hill, a Mongol ruler who gave the title ocean of wisdom. Empty niches at Bamiyan, a sealed cave at Dunhuang, and in Vietnam, a king who became a monk. Then across the oceans: translators carried the texts into English, a poem told the Buddha's life, two Buddhists spoke in Chicago, Zen came west, temples endured, Tibetans taught in exile, insight traveled, and now the sangha is everywhere, even on a screen. Tomorrow a new part of the path begins: the great teachers.
screen: `THE SILK ROAD AND CHINA.` · `KOREA AND JAPAN.` · `TIBET AND MONGOLIA.` · `ACROSS THE OCEANS.` · then, large: `IT TRAVELED FAR.`

segments.voice: With a finger in the air, or only in your mind, trace the road: northern India, over the mountains, east along the Silk Road to China, Korea, then Japan, back to Tibet, out to Mongolia, then across the ocean to the West. At each stop, pause for one breath and let one picture come: a desert, a skull cup, a bronze Buddha, a palace, a hall in Chicago. Then rest, and sit.

Your line: it traveled far. From one tree to many shores. That's the northern roads, done.

956.title: Nagarjuna
956.hook: the second-century Indian philosopher of the middle way and emptiness
956.howItsDone: Nagarjuna's root verses are studied and debated in Tibetan monasteries and read in East Asian schools, and Mahayana Buddhists honor him as a founder of the Madhyamaka, the middle way school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: we closed the northern roads, from India to the West. Your line: it traveled far.

A seed goes into the ground, and a sprout comes up. Is the sprout the same thing as the seed? Not really: the seed is gone. Something completely different, then? Not that either: no seed, no sprout. Same doesn't fit. Different doesn't fit. A thinker from India named Nagarjuna built a whole way of seeing on puzzles like that one. A new part of the path begins today, the great teachers, whose thinking shaped the schools we've followed along the roads. We begin with him.
screen: `A SEED, A SPROUT.` → `NOT THE SAME, NOT DIFFERENT.` → `THE GREAT TEACHERS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Very little about his life is known for sure. Tradition places him in India, centuries after the Buddha, and tells stories about him; one legend says he brought wisdom sutras up from the serpent beings, the nagas, under the sea. Tibetan and East Asian traditions remember him as a founder of the Madhyamaka, the school of the middle. His great work, as tradition counts it, is the Mulamadhyamakakarika, the root verses on the middle way. It starts from the Buddha's teaching that things arise from causes and conditions, and presses on it. If a thing arises only because of other things, it has no being of its own, standing apart. His word for that is shunyata, emptiness. It doesn't mean nothing exists. The sprout is real enough to water. It means nothing exists on its own. In one verse, paraphrased, he says: whatever arises dependently, that is what we call emptiness; it is a name given in dependence, and it is the middle way. Not the extreme that things exist solidly, on their own. Not the extreme that nothing exists at all. The middle. And he warns about his own idea. Elsewhere, again in paraphrase, he says the Buddhas taught emptiness to let go of all views, and those who turn emptiness itself into a view are hard to help. The medicine isn't meant to become another thing to cling to. Even emptiness gets held lightly.
screen: `A TEACHER WRAPPED IN LEGEND.` · `EVERYTHING DEPENDS.` · `EMPTY, BUT NOT NOTHING.` · `HOLD EVEN EMPTINESS LIGHTLY.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY OF EMPTINESS.`

segments.voice: Pick one everyday opinion you carry, about a person, a plan, how today will go, and notice what it leans on: what you heard, what happened last time, how you slept. It's real, and it depends on other things. Loosen your grip on it, the way you'd hold a bird, not a stone, then let it rest, and sit.
Nagarjuna. The teacher from India of the middle way, who said things are empty of being on their own, and warned against clinging even to emptiness.
Your line: the middle way of emptiness. Not solid, not nothing: the middle. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Two truths
957.hook: Nagarjuna: a conventional truth for everyday life, an ultimate truth of emptiness
957.carry: a snake picked up by the wrong end
957.howItsDone: Students in Tibetan monasteries and Mahayana study programs learn the two truths as a core topic of Madhyamaka philosophy, often by memorizing Nagarjuna's verses and debating how the two truths relate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nagarjuna, the teacher of the middle way, who said things are empty of standing on their own. Your line: the middle way of emptiness.

A wooden chair stands by the door. Sit on it and it's plainly a chair: it holds your weight, it scrapes the floor, and if a leg cracks, you fall. Now look a second way. The chair is a tree that grew in rain and sun, a carpenter's hands, glue, nails, and a shape someone named chair. Take those away and no chair is left hiding underneath. Both looks are true. One gets you through the day; the other goes deeper. Nagarjuna had a name for holding both.
screen: `PLAINLY A CHAIR.` → `TREE, HANDS, GLUE, NAILS.` → `BOTH LOOKS ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: In his Root Verses on the Middle Way, Nagarjuna says the Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on two truths. One is conventional truth, the world as we use it every day. The other is ultimate truth, and for Nagarjuna the ultimate is emptiness: nothing exists on its own, from its own side, apart from causes and names. The chair is empty of a separate chair-self. That doesn't make it nothing. It still holds you up. Why keep both? The verses go on: without relying on the everyday, the ultimate can't be taught, and without understanding the ultimate, nirvana isn't reached. So the everyday truth isn't a lie to throw away. It's the ladder. Words, names, kindness, rules for monks, the teaching itself all live in conventional truth, and they're how anyone gets near the ultimate. Then, in the same chapter, a warning. Emptiness wrongly grasped is dangerous, like a snake picked up by the wrong end. Someone who hears that everything is empty and decides nothing matters has grabbed the tail. Buddhist schools read the two truths in more than one way. Tibetan teachers in the Madhyamaka tradition have argued carefully over exactly how the two fit together, and Theravada teachers use a related pair of their own. In Nagarjuna's verses, the shape is this: one world, two ways of seeing it, and the teaching leans on both.
screen: `THE BUDDHAS TEACH BY TWO TRUTHS.` · `ULTIMATE: NOTHING STANDS ON ITS OWN.` · `THE EVERYDAY IS THE LADDER.` · `A SNAKE HELD BY THE WRONG END.` · then, large: `ONE WORLD, TWO WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Choose something within reach, a pen or your own hand, and first let it simply be what it is: name it, and notice what it does for you. Then look the second way, tracing what it's made of, who made it and what it depends on, until no single thing is left standing on its own. Go back and forth slowly with the breath, and let it be a pen again.

Your line: a snake picked up by the wrong end. Emptiness, held well, never makes the day stop mattering. Day nine hundred fifty-seven, done.

958.title: No difference
958.hook: Nagarjuna's famous line: no difference between samsara and nirvana (Mulamadhyamakakarika 25)
958.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists study Nagarjuna's chapter on nirvana in monastic colleges and teaching programs, and some Zen and other East Asian teachers speak of finding awakening in ordinary daily activity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two truths, the everyday and the ultimate, one world seen two ways. Your line: a snake picked up by the wrong end.
screen: `A SNAKE PICKED UP BY THE WRONG END.`

segments.voice: Two words have run underneath this whole path. Samsara: the wheel of birth and death, craving and suffering, round and round. Nirvana: the fire gone out, the wheel stopped, peace. Much of this path has followed the teaching from the first toward the second. Then, near the end of his Root Verses, Nagarjuna writes a line that seems to erase the distance. There's no difference between them, he says. Not the slightest.
screen: `SAMSARA: THE TURNING WHEEL.` → `NIRVANA: THE FIRE GONE OUT.` → `NAGARJUNA CLOSES THE GAP.`

segments.voice: It's in chapter twenty-five, on nirvana. Samsara has not the slightest difference from nirvana, Nagarjuna writes, and nirvana has not the slightest difference from samsara. Then he presses further: the limit of nirvana is the limit of samsara, and between the two there's not even the finest gap. How can he say it? Through yesterday's two truths. In ultimate terms, samsara and nirvana are both empty. Neither is a thing standing on its own, a place you leave or a place you arrive. Nirvana isn't a far country with a border to cross. Now, what the line doesn't say. It doesn't say nothing needs to change, or that craving is already peace. The chapter itself closes by calling peace the stilling of all grasping and all spinning thoughts. The difference he denies is between two separate, solid realms. The work of seeing clearly remains. Readers hear it in different ways. Madhyamaka teachers in India and Tibet read the line through emptiness, with careful logic. In East Asia, some Zen and other Mahayana teachers heard in it something close to home: awakening is found here, in the kitchen and the market, not somewhere else. Each reading takes the line seriously in its own way. And it leaves one question for an ordinary afternoon. If the sacred isn't somewhere else, where is it right now?
screen: `NOT THE SLIGHTEST DIFFERENCE.` · `BOTH ARE EMPTY.` · `THE WORK OF SEEING REMAINS.` · `READ THROUGH LOGIC, READ AT HOME.` · then, large: `NOT EVEN THE FINEST GAP.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes or ears rest on the plainest thing near you, a spoon, a doorframe, the sound of traffic, your own breath. Don't make it special or holy by thinking hard; just give it the kind of attention you might give in a temple or under a great tree. Let it be ordinary, and let it be enough.
No difference. Nagarjuna's line that samsara and nirvana have not the slightest difference, since both are empty of standing on their own. Today's word.
Your line: not even the finest gap. Samsara and nirvana, side by side, with nothing between. See you tomorrow.

959.title: A letter to a king
959.hook: Nagarjuna's letter of advice to a royal friend
959.howItsDone: Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend is studied in Tibetan Buddhism as practical advice for lay life, and teachers often explain the eight worldly concerns from it to lay students.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no difference. Samsara and nirvana, with not even the finest gap between them.

The thinker who wrote of emptiness and two truths also had a friend who was a king. To that friend, tradition says, he wrote a letter. Not a treatise for scholars: a letter, in verse, for a busy man with a kingdom to run. It's known in Sanskrit as the Suhrllekha, the Letter to a Friend, and it survives in Tibetan and Chinese translations. The philosopher of emptiness, writing advice for a Tuesday.
screen: `A PHILOSOPHER WITH A ROYAL FRIEND.` → `A LETTER, IN VERSE.` → `ADVICE FOR A BUSY KING.`

segments.voice: The letter begins humbly. Just as the wise honor an image of the Buddha even when it's carved from plain wood, it says, so please honor this advice, even if the verses are poor. The worth is in what it points to, not the polish. Then it doesn't start with emptiness. It speaks of generosity, of keeping ethical conduct, of patience, of not drinking to excess, and of eating moderately, like taking medicine. Things a king can actually do between meetings. Next come the eight worldly concerns: gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disgrace. The letter asks the king to meet them all evenly, the good four and the hard four alike, since none of them lasts. For a ruler surrounded by flatterers and critics, that's practical advice. And it closes a week. The translators of the Pali Text Society, carrying old words into English. Sitting together, apart, on a screen. A last look back along the Silk Road and beyond. Then Nagarjuna: the middle way, two truths, no difference. And now the same teacher, setting down plain advice in a friendly letter. The hardest ideas of the week still needed someone to write them kindly, for one person.
screen: `HONOR IT LIKE A WOODEN BUDDHA.` · `GENEROSITY, PATIENCE, MODERATION.` · `MEET THE EIGHT CONCERNS EVENLY.` · `A WEEK OF CARRYING THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `A LETTER OF ADVICE.`

segments.voice: In your head, or on paper if one is near, write yourself a short letter of advice, opening the way Nagarjuna did: these are plain words, but take them seriously. Add two or three lines as a friend would, not a judge: one about something you can actually do, one about meeting praise or blame a little more evenly. Then sit quietly with what you wrote.
Suhrllekha. Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend, verses of everyday advice for a king, offered like a Buddha carved from plain wood. Today's word.
Your line: a letter of advice. Gain and loss, praise and blame: all eight come and go. That's the week.
